You are one lens of a verification pass over a completed slice of work. Six of you run, each
blind to the others. Report findings; do not fix anything.

HARD RULES
- Do NOT write, edit or create any file in /home/user/adss-2026-09-07. Do not run git commands that change state
  (no commit, checkout, reset, add, stash). Reading, and the project's own read-only commands,
  are fine. Work in /tmp if you need to write anything.
- You may run: uv run pytest, uv run adss check, uv run ruff check, uv run sqlfluff lint, and
  read-only DuckDB queries against /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/warehouse.duckdb (open it read_only=True).
- Ground every finding in something you actually read or ran. Quote the file and line, or the
  command and its output. A finding you cannot ground is not a finding.
- Severity honestly: "blocking" means the slice should not be accepted as it stands.
  "worth fixing" means fix it but it does not block. "note" is an observation.
- Report NOTHING rather than padding. An empty list from a lens that genuinely found nothing
  is the most useful possible result. Do not manufacture findings to look thorough.

THE REPOSITORY
/home/user/adss-2026-09-07. An analytical data storage system in three layers:
- DAS (das__raw, das__staged): dlt lands whole source records as one JSON column into
  hive-partitioned parquet; contracts generate typed views over it.
- DAB (dab, dab__stage, dab__meta): a focal/ensemble model built by a vendored engine binary.
  dab/model.yaml is the only place the data is explained.
- DAR (dar__uss): a generated Unified Star Schema -- one event bridge, one peripheral per
  entity, one calendar.
- destinations/app.py: a marimo page reading dar__uss only.

SLICE 3 is every commit after 9b34378. It answers: "How many orders shipped per shipping
month, and how many days did they take?" It adds: a SECOND EVENT on the SAME entity (ORDER is
both placed and shipped), so a second stage in the bridge; the first case where an event DID
NOT HAPPEN for some entities (21 of 830 orders never shipped, so they have no shipment row at
all); a value DERIVED from two columns of one row (SHIP_LAG_DAYS, computed in the mapping); and
a ratio that is deliberately NOT stored -- the answer returns two additive measures and the
page divides them. Use: git -C /home/user/adss-2026-09-07 log --oneline 9b34378..HEAD and
git -C /home/user/adss-2026-09-07 diff 9b34378..HEAD

READ THESE FIRST: /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/blueprint.md, /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/conventions.md,
/home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/deviations.md, /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/adr/*.md -- especially docs/adr/0006, which is this
slice's decision and states exactly what the generator is supposed to do and why. They are
the standard you judge against.

LENS -- LAYERING. Does anything read across a boundary it should not?

F1 analytical usage reads only DAR. F2 DAR reads only DAB. F3 DAB reads only DAS.

1. The sharpest question this slice raises: SHIP_LAG_DAYS is ARITHMETIC performed in
   dab/mappings/order-mapping.yaml. ADR 0007 argues that is where it belongs, and draws a line
   -- arithmetic over one row is permitted; a CASE on values, a default, a filter or a bucket
   is not. Read the ADR, then read the mapping, and say whether the line is coherent and
   whether this expression is on the right side of it. Do not wave it through and do not
   reflexively condemn it: argue it.
2. Does the question's uss.sql read only dar__uss? Does staged.sql avoid dab and dar__uss?
   Note that BOTH now compute a lag -- one with date_diff, one from the stored attribute. Is
   the control query still independent of what it checks?
3. Does destinations/app.py still touch nothing but dar__uss and the question files? It now
   performs a division. Is arithmetic in a destination a layering problem or the thing
   conventions section 2 explicitly asks for?
4. checks/*.sql and src/adss/checks.py: same question as before about a conformance check
   spanning layers.
5. Does anything in DAS interpret rather than record?

# Architectural blueprint

This is the overarching document. It states what the system must achieve and the absolute
principles that support it. It names no technology, no tool, no modelling technique and no
process — those live in [conventions.md](conventions.md) and in [adr/](adr/README.md), and each
must justify itself against what is written here.

That separation is the point. Every tool this system currently uses must be replaceable without
invalidating a single line below.

## The vision

An analytical data storage system is built for requirements that do not exist yet, and it is
changed from the inside by its own use: every question it answers expands what its users want to
ask next. It is therefore judged over a life cycle measured in decades, not over the delivery of
any one data product.

Four qualities, in no priority order, because a design that sacrifices one for another is a
design that has failed:

| Quality | What it means here |
|---|---|
| **Maintainable** | A change costs about the same in year ten as in year one. |
| **Scalable** | Adding a source or a consumer strengthens the system rather than making the next addition harder. |
| **Adaptable** | A source replacement, a new entity or a new relationship is absorbed without rewriting what already works. |
| **Good time to market** | Not the fastest possible way. Always within acceptable timing. |

Speed is deliberately last-named and deliberately qualified. A system that answers today's
question fastest and next year's question not at all has optimised the wrong variable.

## The three layers

The layers are named for their **purpose**, never for their position or their quality grade.
They are not bronze, silver and gold; they are not staging, core and marts. Ask three people what
belongs in silver and you get four answers — and these names are also the principles, so a name
that does not carry a principle is a name that cannot be enforced.

| Layer | Data according to… | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **DAS** | the **System** | what the source sent us, as it sent it |
| **DAB** | the **Business** | what the business means by it, integrated and source-agnostic |
| **DAR** | the **Requirements** | what a particular consumer needs, shaped for them |

## Flow

Flow is one-directional and has exactly three rules. They are absolutes.

| # | Rule | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | **Analytical usage reads only DAR.** | Consumption against DAS or DAB creates dependencies on structures whose whole purpose is to be free to change. The dependency is invisible until something breaks. |
| F2 | **DAR reads only DAB.** | A data product that reaches past the business layer to a source has bypassed the integration that makes numbers agree, and reintroduces the cascade the architecture exists to break. |
| F3 | **DAB reads only DAS.** | A source connection wired into the business layer means the source dependency was moved, not broken. |

Each movement between layers does exactly **one** job: ingest, integrate, specialise. Code that
ingests and integrates, or integrates and shapes for a report, has collapsed two layers into one
and is not permitted regardless of how convenient it is.

## Per-layer principles

### DAS — data according to the system

| # | Principle | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | **Capture and persist only.** No business logic, no interpretation, no enrichment. | Interpretation here buries a decision in the one layer that is supposed to make none, and disguises the next source change as a business change. |
| S2 | **Non-volatile.** Nothing is updated. Nothing is deleted. Every load is retained. | DAB and DAR must be rebuildable from DAS at any time without going back to the source. That is what makes changing the layers above it safe. |
| S3 | **Forgiving ingestion, strict unpacking.** Accept whatever arrives; enforce structure at the boundary out. | Committing to a schema at ingest turns every upstream change into lost data. Enforcing nothing on the way out turns every upstream change into a silent one. |
| S4 | **Every data point records where it came from and when.** | Without per-row provenance, an answer that looks wrong cannot be traced, and the only remaining move is to distrust the whole system. |
| S5 | **The source keeps its own words.** | A field renamed to a business term is an interpretation, and S1 forbids interpretations here. |

### DAB — data according to the business

| # | Principle | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| B1 | **Subject oriented.** Organised around business concepts, never around source systems. | The concepts outlive the systems that happen to record them. |
| B2 | **Integrated.** Semantically and structurally source-agnostic. | Adding a second source for a concept must not add a parallel structure, and removing one must not change any structure at all. This is the property that breaks the dependency. |
| B3 | **Time-variant.** Historized: every version retained, none overwritten. | An answer served last quarter must still be reproducible this quarter, or the system cannot be audited. |
| B4 | **Non-volatile.** Never updated, never deleted. | Same reason as B3, stated as a physical constraint rather than an intention. |
| B5 | **Atomic.** The atomic data point is the base of every semantic meaning. No aggregation, no bucketing, no pre-rollup. | An aggregate here is a requirement leaking down a layer, and it is the reason teams start demanding raw data. |
| B6 | **Reusable.** Nothing exists here because one consumer wanted it. | A construct that only makes sense given one requirement belongs in DAR. |
| B7 | **Change is additive.** A new attribute, entity or relationship is a new structure, never a modification of an existing one. | A modification has a regression surface. An addition does not. Repeated over the thousands of changes a platform absorbs, that difference is the whole ball game. |
| B8 | **Meaning is defined exactly once, here.** | Definitions that exist in two places drift, and the drift surfaces as two reports that disagree. |

### DAR — data according to the requirements

| # | Principle | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | **Requirement oriented.** Shaped for a specific consumer, optimised for them. | The integration work is already done; this layer's only job is to be usable. |
| R2 | **No cross-dependency.** A data product owns its structures and does not consume another product's. Duplication between products is accepted deliberately. | Each product has its own rate of change. Sharing structure couples those rates and reintroduces the dependency problem at the consumption layer. |
| R3 | **Reuse the definition, never the instance.** | Consistency comes from a shared *meaning* in DAB, not from a shared *table* here. The conformed dimension buys agreement by sharing structure and pays in coupling; with a real integration layer beneath, that price is unnecessary. |
| R4 | **Volatile and generated.** Nothing here is hand-written or hand-edited. | Anything derived from DAB can be thrown away and rebuilt. An edit to generated output is lost on the next generation, and until then the code and the model quietly disagree. |
| R5 | **What was delivered, to whom, and when is recorded.** | An answer someone acted on must be reconstructable, including the definitions that produced it. |

## What structure cannot do

Generation guarantees **consistency**, not **correctness**. A poorly chosen model compiles just
as reliably as a good one, and a system that enforces coherent structure over incoherent
definitions produces coherent-looking incoherence — which is more dangerous than visible mess,
because it is trusted.

Deciding what an entity is, when two records refer to the same instance, and whether two
attributes carry the same meaning remains human judgement. The effort saved on mechanism is meant
to be redirected to meaning, not removed.

## No exceptions

This document contains no exceptions and no pre-authorised bypass. That is deliberate: if a
principle is not stated as an absolute, with its reason recorded, there is nothing to break, and
a deviation becomes indistinguishable from an ordinary decision.

Reality still wins sometimes. When it does, the answer is not to weaken the principle but to
**cost the deviation**: which principle breaks, why the conforming option was unworkable here,
what it costs, and the observable condition under which it is removed. That record lives in
[deviations.md](deviations.md), and every deviation has an ADR behind it.

16	## How to read a rule
17	
18	Every rule carries a **why** and a severity. The why is not decoration: it is what lets a
19	reviewer tell a genuine violation from a case the rule was never aimed at.
20	
21	| Severity | Meaning | On a pull request |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| **Hard rule** | Breaking it breaks a contract something else depends on. | Blocks. Fix it, or register a deviation with an ADR. |

26	## 1. Naming by layer
27	
28	Names are the interface between layers, so each layer names things in its own vocabulary and
29	never in its neighbour's.
30	
31	The layers are called `das`, `dab` and `dar` literally — in schemas, in directories, in prose.
32	Never bronze/silver/gold, never staging/core/marts. The name carries the principle
33	([blueprint.md](blueprint.md)); a name that carries no principle cannot be enforced.
34	
35	### 1.1 DAS — the source-vocabulary exemption
36	
37	| Rule | Why | Severity |
38	|---|---|---|
39	| DAS object and column names mirror the source. The source's own words are **required** here, even where other layers forbid them. | DAS exists to say what the source said. Renaming a source field to a business term buries an interpretation in the layer that must make none. | Hard rule |
40	| The mechanical translation is expected: a source property becomes `snake_case`, a source entity set becomes a `snake_case` plural table named after the source's own word for it. | A consistent spelling of the source's word is still the source's word. | Hard rule |
41	| A contract file's stem is the landed table name, and that name is used in every schema of this layer. | One name for one thing, so grepping for a table finds its contract. | Hard rule |
42	| A source name that would be a violation anywhere else — `ShipVia`, `total_orders` — is **not** a violation here. | It is a column in a table nobody on this side controls. A rule that cannot tell that case from a name we chose produces false accusations. | Hard rule |
43	| A contract's `description` stays in system vocabulary: the source's type, its nullability, what the source calls it. Never what it means to the business. | Business meaning has exactly one home (§1.2). | Hard rule |
44	| Columns this layer adds itself carry no source's word and are named for what they record: `payload`, `source_system`, `source_entity`, `source_url`, `extracted_at`, `extracted_on`. | Provenance is ours, not the source's, and must be tellable apart from it at a glance. | Hard rule |

81	### 1.4 DAB — mapping rules
82	
83	A mapping says how one entity is loaded from DAS. These rules exist because daana accepts several
84	kinds of wrong mapping without complaint, and two of them corrupt data silently.
85	
86	| # | Rule | Why | Severity |
87	|---|---|---|---|
88	| M1 | `table:` names a `das__staged` object and nothing else. Never a subquery, never a join, never `das__raw`. | Blueprint F3. A join here is business logic in the wrong layer; a raw read skips the contract's casts and the contract stops being the gate. | Hard rule |
89	| M2 | Exactly **one** `primary_keys` entry, whose VARCHAR result is the entity key: a bare string column, `cast(col AS VARCHAR)`, or a `concat` of casts with a separator. | Two entries are two *alternate identifiers* to daana, not a composite key, and that mode cannot be undone once loaded. A `concat` without a separator makes `'A1' + '23'` and `'A12' + '3'` the same key. | Hard rule |
90	| M3 | `ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG`. `FULL` is permitted only against a source view **proven** to hold exactly one row per key, and the proof is a data check, not a claim. | Observed: `FULL` against a multi-row-per-key source inserts one duplicate `_desc` row per execute, forever, and every presentation view hides it. Our staged change log is multi-row-per-key by construction, so `FULL` is the wrong default here and the failure is invisible. | Hard rule |
91	| M4 | `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at`. | Blueprint B3. The effective time of a fact is when DAS observed it. Anything else dates the fact by something that is not about the fact — and no source here reports when it changed. | Hard rule |
92	| M5 | An attribute expression reads its own row: a column, a cast, a `CASE` over columns of that row, or **arithmetic over columns of that row** — including a same-row function such as `date_diff`. Never a subquery, never an aggregate, never a reach into another table. | An expression that reaches beyond the row is a join, and every join must come from a declared relationship. Arithmetic over one row produces a value the row already implies, so it needs no definition of its own beyond the attribute it lands in. | Hard rule |
93	| M5a | What arithmetic does **not** cover: a `CASE` on *values*, a default, a coalesce that invents one, a filter, a bucket, or anything that changes the grain. Those go in the model as an attribute with a definition. | Each of them is a choice somebody made, and a choice needs a definition beside it. The mechanical check cannot tell arithmetic from a bucket — it is four keywords and seven function names — so this line is the rule and the regex is only its cheapest half. ADR 0007. | Hard rule |
94	| M6 | A relationship's `id` is `<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`; its `source_table` is byte-identical to a `table` in its mapping; its target expression has the same **shape** as the target entity's own key expression — the same casts and the same functions, though the column may be named differently. Every edge the model declares is loaded by some mapping, and every edge a mapping loads is declared by the model. | A mismatched `source_table` is skipped silently, and a key of a different shape produces pairs that join to nothing. Neither says anything at load time. The shape is what matters and the spelling is not: a foreign key is routinely named differently from the primary key it points at, and it is the casting and the functions that decide the VARCHAR the two sides produce. | Hard rule |
95	| M7 | Every mapped table carries at least one attribute. | daana refuses to deploy an entity with none, and the failure arrives at deploy rather than at review. | Hard rule |

100	## 2. Measure naming
101	
102	The most consequential convention here, and the one to get right first.
103	
104	**Pattern: `<descriptor>_<entities>_<unit>`.**
105	
106	| Rule | Why | Severity |
107	|---|---|---|
108	| Three parts in that order: what distinguishes it, the entity it counts or sums over, the unit it is in. | Three fixed slots make names comparable at a glance and searchable by any of the three. | Hard rule |
109	| The entity part is **plural**: `orders`, `order_lines`. | A measure is always about a set. The singular is reserved for the entity itself. | Hard rule |
110	| Scope and aggregation words never appear: no `total_`, `sum_`, `avg_`, `count_of_`, `num_`, `_ytd`, `_by_month`. | Aggregation and scope are chosen by the query, not baked into the name. `total_orders` is a lie the moment somebody filters it. | Hard rule |
111	| The unit is a real unit: `count`, `amount`, `days`. | It is what tells a reader whether two measures can be added. | Hard rule |
112	| **Ratios are not stored.** Store numerator and denominator as additive measures and divide at query time. | An average of averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at. | Hard rule |
113	| A name must be self-explanatory without a glossary lookup, and must describe the business concept rather than the implementation. | If understanding a measure needs the glossary open, the name has failed at the only job a name has. | Guideline |
114	| No abbreviations. `paid_subscriptions_count`, not `nbr_of_paid_subs`. | Abbreviations are unsearchable, and searchability is most of a name's value. | Guideline |
115	
116	| Instead of | Write | Because |
117	|---|---|---|
118	| `total_orders` | `placed_orders_count` | Scope word goes; the descriptor says *which* orders; the unit says what the number is. |
119	| `sum_revenue` | `revenue_order_lines_amount` | `sum` is the query's job; the entity says at what grain revenue is measured. |
120	| `avg_days_to_ship` | `ship_lag_orders_days` | The average is `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time, from two additive measures. |

122	## 3. SQL style
123	
124	Everything a tool can check is checked by `sqlfluff` with [`.sqlfluff`](../.sqlfluff); this page
125	records why the settings are what they are. All hard rules, because generated and hand-written
126	SQL have to be indistinguishable to a reviewer.
127	
128	| Rule | Why |
129	|---|---|
130	| Dialect is `duckdb`. | Not a preference: the `postgres` dialect cannot parse `QUALIFY`. |
131	| Keywords upper case, functions lower case, identifiers lower case. | Three visual classes, so structure, computation and data separate at a glance in a long generated statement. |
132	| Four-space indent; one selected expression per line; every expression aliased with `AS`. | Diffs of generated SQL are read constantly. One expression per line makes a one-column change a one-line diff. |
133	| Every table reference has an explicit alias, and a join condition names the earlier table first. | Reading order matches join order, so a wrong join key is visible without tracing back up the statement. |
134	| `cast(x AS T)`, never `x::T`. | `CV11` enforces one casting style; `cast()` is the one that reads as a function like every other function. |
135	| Every column reference in a multi-table statement is table-qualified. | `RF02`. It is the one rule sqlfluff cannot autofix, and it is a correctness rule, not a style one. |
136	| Identifiers crossing over from DAB are double-quoted; everything this repository creates is lower case and unquoted, except reserved words. | The two conventions must be visually distinct, because a mixed-case identifier that loses its quotes fails only at run time. |
137	| No `SELECT *` in anything a consumer reads, except a union of stages whose column list the generator fixes. | A star is a schema change waiting to be silent. |
138	| SQL that lives in a Python string is written to a file so the same linter sees it. | A rule that applies only to the SQL somebody remembered to put in a `.sql` file is not a rule. |
139	| Every `read_parquet` over the lake passes `union_by_name => true` and `hive_types` for the partition column. | Both are correctness, not taste. Without the first, a column that appears only in later loads is **silently dropped** — no error, just missing data. Without the second, the partition key comes back VARCHAR. |
140	| Every path in a persisted view is absolute. | A relative path inside a view resolves against the process's working directory at **query** time, not at create time, so a view created from the repository root breaks the moment a page opens the same warehouse from elsewhere. |
141	
142	Four rules are excluded, and the reasons are in [`.sqlfluff`](../.sqlfluff): `AL09` forbids
143	`x AS x`, which is exactly the every-column-aliased discipline that makes a `UNION` branch
144	positionally safe; `RF06` fires on every mixed-case identifier crossing over from DAB; `LT05` and
145	`LT09` are line-layout opinions a generator should not have to implement.

170	## 6. Tests
171	
172	There are **two suites**, and they are not run at the same time or by the same thing.
173	
174	| Suite | What it is | When it runs |
175	|---|---|---|
176	| **machinery** (`tests/`) | Pure functions over data files. No warehouse, no network, no binary. | Every commit, by the pre-commit gate and by CI. |
177	| **checks** (`checks/`) | Assertions about what the built warehouse actually contains. | After `adss build`, by CI and on demand. |
178	
179	The split is not fastidiousness. The warehouse is not committed, so a data check in the gate
180	would fail in every fresh checkout — and §6's own rules forbid both of the ways out of that (a
181	skip, or a stub to assert against). Naming the two suites is what lets "every commit is green"
182	stay true.
183	
184	| Rule | Why | Severity |
185	|---|---|---|
186	| Machinery is test-first: the failing test and the code that passes it land in one commit. | A test written afterwards is a test that has only ever been seen to pass. | Hard rule |
187	| A data check is never written against a stub or a fabricated warehouse. It asserts what the real build produced, and lands in the same commit as the build step that satisfies it. | TDD is for functions. A check that passes against a stub tells you nothing about the build. | Hard rule |
188	| No `pytest.skip`, no imperative `xfail()` in a test body. | A skip is a test that silently does not exist. An imperative `xfail` can never report an unexpected pass, so it cannot tell you the day the bug is fixed. | Hard rule |
189	| No test contains an entity, attribute, measure, source or column name from the business. Fixtures are neutral models held as **data files**; the question runner discovers question files and asserts over them without naming anything. | The machinery must work for any business; a business name in a test is proof that it does not. A per-question test *function* smuggles the vocabulary back in through its own name — so the runner is parameterised. | Hard rule |
190	| A failing check is fixed by fixing the code, or by making the configuration honest. Never by weakening the test. | A weakened test costs the same to run and reports the opposite of the truth. | Hard rule |
191	| **When a question's two queries disagree, `dab/model.yaml` is the arbiter.** The query that departs from the definition is the one that changes. Never adjust both until they match. | With two hand-written expressions of one question, "fix the code" is ambiguous by construction. Without a named arbiter, the cheapest repair is to make the check agree with itself, which deletes the only thing it was measuring. | Hard rule |

216	## 9. The warehouse has exactly one writer
217	
218	The lock is **per process**. Within one process every connection shares an instance, so a
219	second open succeeds; across processes the second is refused. That distinction is the whole of
220	this section, and getting it backwards costs an afternoon.
221	
222	| Rule | Why | Severity |
223	|---|---|---|
224	| This process must not hold the warehouse open while a separate process is asked to write to it. `require_detached` enforces it rather than asking anyone to remember. | The modelling engine is a separate process. While we hold the file it cannot take the lock, and it reports that as `daana framework is not installed on the remote database` — which is not what went wrong. Reproduced with DuckDB alone, no engine involved. | Hard rule |
225	| Every destination opens the warehouse with `read_only=True`. | A read-only handle still holds the process lock, so a page left open blocks the next build; read-only at least keeps a reader from writing. | Hard rule |
226	| `daana framework is not installed on the remote database` means **the file is busy**. | The real lock error is swallowed and does not appear even at debug level. Anyone meeting this message will otherwise spend an afternoon reinstalling a framework that is already installed. | Hard rule |

8	# A value derived from one row is modelled in DAB and computed in the mapping, and arithmetic there is bounded by this record
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	"How many days did they take" is the first number this system reports that does not exist in the
13	source. Every measure so far has been a count — one per row — or a sum of a single attribute that
14	was already there. A ship lag is two dates subtracted, and there is no established place to put
15	the subtraction.
16	
17	Three things are already settled and an argument that reopens them has not read the standard.
18	
19	**The measure's name and its arithmetic are written down.** Conventions §2's own worked example is
20	this question:
21	
22	> | `avg_days_to_ship` | `ship_lag_orders_days` | The average is
23	> `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time, from two additive
24	> measures. |
25	
26	So the two measures are named, the division is a question's job, and `ship_lag_orders_days` is a
27	*stored measure* — a column in the bridge's published contract. That sentence decides more of this
28	slice than anything else in the repository.
29	
30	**An event that did not happen is already decided.** ADR 0002: "A transaction stage reads
31	`dab.view_<E>_hist`, keeps the latest version in which the event's date is set… An unshipped order
32	therefore has no shipment event *by construction* rather than by a filter somebody has to
33	remember." The generator emits `WHERE <date> IS NOT NULL` and a test pins it. The 21 unshipped
34	orders are the case that design was written for, not a new problem.
35	
36	**Two events on one entity already work.** The neutral fixture has declared two events on one
37	entity since slice 1, and generating this slice's bridge from a scratch copy of the model needs
38	**no generator change at all**. What is new is one thing only: a sum measure with no attribute to
39	point at.
40	
41	## Decision Drivers
42	
43	* a number the business reads has exactly one definition, in the one place data is explained
44	* the acceptance check keeps an arbiter: when two queries disagree, something decides which is wrong
45	* the precedent this sets is one the next three slices can live with
46	* a rule the next person inherits, rather than an example they have to interpret
47	* DAR stays a layer that can be deleted and rebuilt from the model
48	
49	## Considered Options
50	
51	* **(a)** A `NUMBER` attribute on `ORDER`, computed in the mapping from two columns of its own row
52	* **(b)** An expression in `dab/uss.yaml`, emitted into the bridge by the generator
53	* **(c)** Computed in the question's `uss.sql` at query time from two dates on the peripheral
54	
55	## Decision Outcome
56	
57	Chosen: **(a), a `NUMBER` attribute computed in the mapping** — with the precedent bounded here,
58	because "M5 permits it" is otherwise the standing argument for whatever M5's regex happens not to
59	catch.
60	
61	It is also the only option that generates today. A `sum` measure must name an attribute the model
62	declares; `src/adss/uss.py` raises `KeyError: "ORDER has no attribute …"` otherwise, and there is
63	no `expression:` field on a measure. (b) and (c) are not choices between working designs — they
64	are proposals to build something.
65	
66	**Why not (b).** Putting the arithmetic in the generator is the serious rival, and it is cleaner in
67	one respect: nothing derived is stored, so nothing derived can drift. It fails on where it leaves
68	slice 6. A second source that reports elapsed days *directly* has no two dates for a DAR expression
69	to subtract, so integrating it needs the attribute anyway — and then there are two definitions of
70	ship lag, a DAB attribute and a DAR expression, differing by source. That is B2 and B8 failing
71	together in the slice whose entire purpose is to prove B2. It also costs slice 4, where the
72	expression vocabulary would have to grow from a two-date special case to general arithmetic in the
73	same slice that first exercises the fan-out property D-0001 is carried on. Two risky things at once.
74	
75	A free-text SQL expression in YAML additionally breaks §3 — "SQL that lives in a Python string is
76	written to a file so the same linter sees it" — because the linter runs on `.sql` files and would
77	never see it.
78	
79	**Why not (c).** Conventions §2 says ratios are not stored and the numerator *is* an additive
80	measure; (c) reads it as licence for the whole computation and has no `ship_lag_orders_days` at
81	all. The question could then not declare what it measures: every `defines` entry must resolve to
82	something the model or the sidecar defines, so "days to ship" would exist in one SQL file and
83	nowhere else, with the page's own glossary unable to explain the second number it displays.
84	
85	The fatal objection is narrower. §6: "When a question's two queries disagree, `dab/model.yaml` is
86	the arbiter. The query that departs from the definition is the one that changes." Under (c) the
87	answer query says `date_diff('day', o.placed_on, o.shipped_on)`, the control says
88	`shipped_date - order_date`, and the model has nothing to say about either. Neither query can
89	depart from a definition that does not exist, so the repair procedure stops existing in exactly the
90	slice that introduces the first computed number — and the cheapest repair becomes making the two
91	queries agree with each other, which deletes the only thing the check measures.
92	
93	(c) also computes as of the wrong instant: the peripheral is current state, while a bridge row is
94	the latest version *in which the event's date is set*. Those coincide today. ADR 0006 records a
95	review catching precisely this confusion one layer down, and calls the distinction the entire
96	difference between the option chosen there and the one rejected.
97	
98	### The line this record draws
99	
100	M5 permits an expression that reads its own row, and its prose enumerates three forms — a column,
101	a cast, a `CASE` over columns of that row. A subtraction of two dates is none of them, and passes
102	only because M5's mechanical check is four keywords and seven function names. Relying on that
103	silently is the quiet exception §11 rules out. So the rule, in force from here:
104	
105	> **Arithmetic over columns of the same row is permitted in a mapping.** A `CASE` on *values*, a
106	> default, a coalesce that invents a value, a filter, a bucket, or anything that changes the grain
107	> is not — those are meaning, and meaning belongs in the model as an attribute with a definition.
108	
109	Conventions §1.4 M5 is clarified to say so, per §11's first rung. The distinction is that
110	arithmetic over one row produces a value the row already implies; the others produce a value
111	somebody chose, and a choice needs a definition beside it.
112	
113	One trap belongs in the record because the error message misleads: `extract(DAY FROM (b - a))` is
114	**refused** by M5's checker, because the regex matches the bare word `from` inside the expression.
115	The refusal says the expression "reaches beyond its row", which it does not. `date_diff('day', a,
116	b)` passes and is what the mapping uses. The false refusal is a defect in the checker, fixed in
117	this slice.
118	
119	## Consequences
120	
121	* Good, because the lag has one definition, in the one place the data is explained, and both of the
122	  question's queries are measured against it
123	* Good, because a second source that reports the lag directly maps onto the same attribute rather
124	  than needing a second derivation — which is the slice-6 case that decided this
125	* Good, because slice 4's revenue follows the same rule without a new mechanism: quantity, price
126	  and discount are columns of one order line, and their product is arithmetic over that row
127	* Good, because DAR stays deletable: everything it emits still comes from the model and the sidecar
128	* Bad, because a derived value is now stored, and a stored derivation can disagree with what it was
129	  derived from. Nothing today can make that happen — one mapping, one source — and it becomes
130	  possible in slice 6
131	* Bad, because the line above is a rule enforced by review. M5's checker cannot tell arithmetic
132	  from a bucket, and writing a checker that could is a bigger thing than this slice needs
133	
134	## Confirmation
135	
136	`tests/test_mapping_rules.py` asserts that a same-row function is accepted and that the reaching
137	forms are still refused, including the `extract(… FROM …)` case that used to be refused for the
138	wrong reason.
139	
140	The two measures are `SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT` and `SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS`, and the ratio appears in no
141	schema: the question returns both additive measures and the page divides them. That is not only
142	§2's rule but what keeps the acceptance check exact — every value either query returns is a
143	`BIGINT` count or an exact `DECIMAL` sum, and the two answers are compared row by row as values.
144	A float would break that comparison in a way no test would find on the machine that wrote it:
145	DuckDB's `sum` over doubles is order-dependent, measured here as `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` summing to
146	`0.6000000000000001` and the same three reversed to `0.6`. `tests/test_questions.py` pins that
147	every question's answer holds only exact types, so the first float-valued measure fails a test
148	rather than producing a disagreement that is not one.
149	
150	What is **not** confirmed, and is recorded rather than claimed: nothing checks that
151	`SHIP_LAG_DAYS` still equals the two dates it was derived from. Such a check is tautological
152	today — one mapping computes it from those columns and nothing else writes it — and stops being
153	tautological in slice 6, which is the slice this decision's one real risk lands in. It is not
154	written now because a check that cannot fail teaches a reader that the property is guarded when it
155	is not; slice 6 writes it, against the case that makes it meaningful.

8	# A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity, so two events on one entity may not name the same measure
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	Slice 3 is the first slice where one entity has two events: an order is both placed and shipped.
13	That splits two things which have been the same thing until now.
14	
15	A measure's **column** and its **glossary token** are keyed on the entity:
16	
17	```python
18	(event, measure, f"_measure__{event.entity_id.lower()}__{measure.id.lower()}")
19	found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
20	```
21	
22	Its **ownership** is keyed on the event — `_branch` decides which stage carries a value and which
23	emits a typed null by identity on the event object. So the generator knows exactly which stage owns
24	a measure, and then names it after something else.
25	
26	With one event per entity those keys coincide and nothing can go wrong. With two, declaring the
27	same measure id on both events of one entity is accepted without a word, and produces:
28	
29	- **the same column twice** in the published contract, and
30	- **one definition silently replacing the other** in the glossary.
31	
32	Reproduced on the neutral fixture. The column list came back with
33	`_measure__parent__happened_parents_count` at two positions, and the glossary held the *second*
34	event's definition under the first event's token.
35	
36	The two halves fail very differently. DuckDB does not refuse two columns of one name — measured,
37	`CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS a` yields `a` and `a_1` — so the built table's columns would
38	not match `bridge_columns()` and the contract check would fail the build loudly. That half is safe.
39	
40	**The glossary half is caught by nothing.** No check inspects `definitions()`. That dictionary is
41	what a question's `defines` entries are resolved against, and what the page renders as "What the
42	words mean". So a question could reference a measure, resolve it successfully, and be shown a
43	definition belonging to a different measure — on the page a reader accepts the slice on — while
44	every test and every check passes.
45	
46	Nothing enforces the naming convention that would prevent it either. Conventions §2's three-part
47	pattern is a hard rule, and there is no test anywhere that checks a measure name's shape. The
48	uniqueness of these columns has rested entirely on a rule enforced by reading.
49	
50	## Decision Drivers
51	
52	* a definition that is silently replaced is worse than one that is missing: nothing looks wrong
53	* the failure must be loud where it is invisible, not only where DuckDB happens to complain
54	* a published column contract two consumers are already written against
55	* whatever is decided now is cheapest now, with two questions in existence
56	
57	## Considered Options
58	
59	* Refuse the collision when the declarations are read, and keep the entity in the column name
60	* Rename the column to `_measure__<event>__<measure>` and the token to `<ENTITY>.<EVENT>.measures.<M>`
61	* Do nothing, and rely on §2's naming pattern to keep ids distinct
62	
63	## Decision Outcome
64	
65	Chosen: **refuse the collision when the declarations are read.**
66	
67	Two events on one entity may not declare the same measure id. The refusal names both events and
68	says what would be lost, because the loss is not obvious: a reader who has just been told the
69	column would be duplicated will think of the column, and the definition is the part nothing else
70	would catch.
71	
72	**Why not rename to the event.** It is more correct in principle — the event is what actually owns
73	a measure, so the name should say so — and it is the cheapest it will ever be, with only two
74	questions to update. It is rejected on two counts. It changes a published contract that conventions
75	§1.3 states as a hard rule and ADR 0002 tabulates, in a slice that has no other reason to touch it.
76	And §2's descriptor slot already carries the event: `placed_orders_count`, `shipped_orders_count`.
77	Naming the column for the event too would put it in twice, so the more correct scheme reads worse
78	in every ordinary case in order to disambiguate one that is now refused outright.
79	
80	**Why not do nothing.** §2's pattern makes a collision unlikely, not impossible, and "unlikely" is
81	the wrong guarantee for a failure whose signature is a page showing a plausible sentence about the
82	wrong number. Two events on one entity is exactly where the pattern's descriptor slot stops doing
83	the work — `placed` and `shipped` distinguish the count measures, and nothing forces a third
84	measure to carry a descriptor at all.
85	
86	This follows the shape the repository already uses for the same class of problem: ADR 0006 refuses
87	two edges that would inherit into one key column, for the same reason and with the same argument
88	about what DuckDB silently does instead of raising. A generator that cannot emit a correct artefact
89	should say so rather than emit an ambiguous one.
90	
91	## Consequences
92	
93	* Good, because the glossary can no longer show one measure's definition under another's name,
94	  which was the only failure here that nothing would have reported
95	* Good, because it is a refusal in the same place and the same shape as the one for colliding
96	  edges, so the two read as one rule rather than two special cases
97	* Good, because it costs nothing today: no existing declaration collides, and no column moves
98	* Bad, because it forbids a legitimate-sounding declaration — the same quantity measured at two
99	  events, deliberately, under one name. That would have to be two measures with two definitions,
100	  which is more honest but more typing. If a slice ever wants it, the answer is to rename to the
101	  event, and this record is what it supersedes
102	* Bad, because the deeper mismatch stays: the generator still names by entity what it owns by
103	  event. This narrows the consequence to nothing rather than removing the cause
104	
105	## Confirmation
106	
107	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts that two events on one entity declaring one measure id are refused,
108	and that the same id on two *different* entities is still accepted — which is the case the
109	refusal must not catch, since `_measure__<entity>__` already distinguishes those.
110	
111	A second test asserts that `definitions()` returns one entry per declared measure, so a future
112	change that reintroduces a silent overwrite fails on the count rather than on somebody reading a
113	page carefully. That is the assertion that would have caught this, and it did not exist.
114

1	# Deviations register
2	
3	Every knowing departure from a principle in [blueprint.md](blueprint.md) or a hard rule in
4	[conventions.md](conventions.md) is recorded here, with the ADR that decided it.
5	
6	The register exists because an unregistered exception is indistinguishable from a mistake. Once
7	one exists, the next person reads it as precedent and copies it, and a year later the rule is
8	folklore. Writing the cost down keeps the trade visible; writing an exit condition down keeps it
9	from becoming permanent by default.
10	
11	A deviation is legitimate only when all four fields are answerable. If the cost cannot be named,
12	the deviation has not been understood. If the exit condition cannot be named, it is not a
13	deviation but a change of rule, and the rule should be superseded instead.
14	
15	## Entries
16	
17	| # | Rule deviated from | Why | Cost | Exit condition | ADR | Status |
18	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
19	| D-0001 | [blueprint.md](blueprint.md) **R2 — No cross-dependency**: "a data product owns its structures and does not consume another product's" | Every slice's page reads one generated Unified Star Schema in `dar__uss`. The structure being shared is additive by construction — keys inherit along many-to-one relationships, measures stay on the stage that owns them — so the fan trap R2 exists to prevent cannot occur in it, and one shared calendar is what lets two processes be compared at all. Generating a private copy per page would make that comparison a cross-schema join, which is most of what a USS is for | A change made for one reader is visible to all of them the moment it is generated. There is no per-reader projection, so "this reader may not see freight" cannot be expressed. Two readers cannot hold different definitions of the same measure. The first thing to break is a slice needing a measure defined one way for one reader and another way for another — it will have to be modelled as two measures | A second consumer needs isolation: a different shape of the same structure, or a group that must not see part of it. The generator then gains per-group projections over the same bridge and this entry is resolved | [0002](adr/0002-dar-is-one-generated-unified-star-schema.md) | open |
20	
21	## Entry format
22	
23	Entries are appended in the order they are decided and never removed. A resolved deviation is
24	marked resolved, with the date and the commit or ADR that resolved it, because the history of why
25	something looked necessary is worth as much as the fact that it no longer is.
26	
27	Field by field:
28	
29	* **Rule deviated from** — quote or link the exact rule. "The spirit of layering" is not a rule;
30	  a row in a blueprint table is.
31	* **Why** — the constraint that made the conforming option unworkable *here*. Convenience, time
32	  pressure and unfamiliarity are not constraints; they are reasons to do it properly.
33	* **Cost** — what this buys the system in trouble. Name the first thing that will break, who pays
34	  for it, and which future change it makes more expensive. A deviation with no cost is evidence
35	  the rule is wrong, so supersede the rule instead of deviating from it.
36	* **Exit condition** — the observable thing that has to become true for the deviation to be
37	  removed. "When we have time" is not observable.
38	* **ADR** — the decision record that argued it. Every deviation has one; the register is the
39	  index, the ADR is the argument.
40	* **Status** — `open` while it stands, `resolved` once it is gone.
41	
42	## Review
43	
44	The register is read at the start of every slice. Each open entry is checked against its exit
45	condition **and against whether its argument is still being carried on assertion** — D-0001's
46	justification rests on measures not multiplying across a walk over many-to-one edges. Slice 2
47	built the first edge, so the walk is now exercised; the property it is supposed to protect is
48	not, because both entities on that edge are at the same grain and no measure *can* multiply
49	across it. The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the
50	argument stops being carried on assertion. ADR 0006 says the same in as many words. An entry should also be re-read the moment a second consumer appears, not only
51	when isolation is demanded, because by then the shared structure will already have shaped both
52	readers. An entry whose exit condition has been met and which is still open is a defect in the
53	same way a failing test is: the system is no longer doing what its own documentation says.

## Story

As the **operations manager**, I want to see how many orders went out each month and how long
they waited, so that I can tell whether a busy month is also a slow one — and staff against the
answer rather than against a feeling.

## Definitions

Every term below is defined in `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` and nowhere else. This
question references them; it does not restate them.

- {{ORDER.SHIPPED_ON}}
- {{ORDER.SHIP_LAG_DAYS}}
- {{ORDER.events.SHIPPED}}
- {{ORDER.measures.SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT}}
- {{ORDER.measures.SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS}}

## The W's

- **Why**: throughput and speed move together or they do not, and which of the two it is
  decides whether the answer is more people or a different process. One number cannot say.
- **What**: two additive measures — the count of orders that went out, and the days they spent
  waiting, added up. Not an average: see below.
- **Who**: the operations manager acts on it; the business ships.
- **How**: one `shipped` event per order, on the day the goods left. **An order that has not
  shipped has no shipment event at all**, so it is absent rather than counted as a zero-day
  order — which would make the slowest orders look like the fastest. 21 of 830 orders are in
  that position.
- **Where**: not asked. This is a question about time, and adding a geography to it would be
  a different question.
- **When**: all history, by the month the goods **left** (`_calendar.month_label`, `YYYY-MM`).
  An order accepted in one month and shipped in the next belongs to the second.
- **What will you do with it**: compare the two lines. A month where the count rises and the
  wait rises with it is a capacity problem; a month where the wait rises on its own is not.

## Why the answer has no average in it

The question asks how many days orders took, and the answer does not contain that number.

Conventions §2: *"Ratios are not stored. Store numerator and denominator as additive measures
and divide at query time."* Its worked example is this question — `avg_days_to_ship` becomes
`ship_lag_orders_days`, and the average is `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)`.
An average of averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at, so a stored
monthly average could not be re-summed into a quarter. Two additive measures can.

There is a second reason, found by measuring rather than by reading. The acceptance check
compares the two answers **row by row as values**, which is exact only while every value is
exact. A ratio is a `DOUBLE` however it is reached. Both queries agree today because both
reduce to one division of two exact integer sums — but float addition is not associative and
DuckDB imposes no order on `sum`: `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` sums to `0.6000000000000001` and the same
three reversed to `0.6`. So the first float-valued measure would let the two queries disagree
by a bit, on some machines, some of the time. Keeping the division out of the stored answer
keeps this check exact by construction rather than by luck.

The page does the division, once, where a reader can see it.

## Nulls

`shipped_date` is null on 21 orders and that is the whole point of this slice: those orders have
no row in the `shipped` stage, by construction rather than by a filter anyone has to remember.
The control query mirrors it with `WHERE o.shipped_date IS NOT NULL`.

No order in the recording ships before it was accepted, and none has a null order date, so no
lag is negative and none is missing on a shipped order. Both queries would carry a null lag
through `sum`, which skips it — so a shipped order with no accepted date would be counted and
not waited-for, in both answers alike.

## Answers

Two queries, in `staged.sql` and `uss.sql`. The first computes the answer straight from what
the source sent, bypassing the business model and the star schema entirely. The second computes
it from the star schema. They must agree row for row — 23 months, 809 orders, 6,870 days.
=====USS=====
-- The answer, from the generated star schema. This is what the destination reads.
--
-- Two additive measures, and no ratio. The wait of a typical order is the second divided by
-- the first, and that division belongs to whoever asks -- conventions section 2. It also
-- keeps this comparison exact: every value here is a count or an exact decimal, and a float
-- would make the two answers disagree by a bit, since summing doubles is order-dependent.
SELECT
    cal.month_label AS shipping_month,
    cast(sum(b._measure__order__shipped_orders_count) AS BIGINT) AS shipped_orders_count,
    cast(sum(b._measure__order__ship_lag_orders_days) AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS ship_lag_orders_days
FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key
WHERE b._event = 'shipped'
GROUP BY cal.month_label
ORDER BY shipping_month
=====STAGED=====
-- The control. Straight from what the source sent, bypassing the business model and the
-- star schema. It may not mention dab or dar__uss: independence is the whole value.
SELECT
    strftime(o.shipped_date, '%Y-%m') AS shipping_month,
    count(*) AS shipped_orders_count,
    cast(sum(date_diff('day', o.order_date, o.shipped_date)) AS DECIMAL(28, 8))
        AS ship_lag_orders_days
FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o
WHERE o.shipped_date IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY strftime(o.shipped_date, '%Y-%m')
ORDER BY shipping_month

259	        # engine skips the relationship in silence and every inherited key is null.
260	        generated[f"{name}__loaded"] = (

262	            f"SELECT count(*) AS unloaded\n"
263	            f"FROM (SELECT 1 AS declared) AS edge\n"
264	            f"WHERE NOT EXISTS (\n"
265	            f"    SELECT 1\n"
266	            f"    {open_pairs}\n"
267	            f");\n"
268	        )

271	        generated[f"{name}__resolves"] = (
272	            f"{_EDGE}\n"
273	            f"SELECT count(*) AS dangling\n"
274	            f"FROM {BRIDGE.sql} AS b\n"
275	            f"LEFT JOIN {Relation(Schema.DAR_USS, target.object_name).sql} AS t\n"
276	            f"    ON b.{target.key_column} = t.{target.key_column}\n"
277	            f"WHERE b._stage = '{source.object_name}'\n"
278	            f"    AND b.{target.key_column} IS NOT NULL\n"
279	            f"    AND t.{target.key_column} IS NULL;\n"
280	        )

# What the source sends, what it is called here, and what type it becomes. This file is the
# documentation, the schema and the transformation; there is nothing beside it to keep in
# step. Descriptions stay in the source's vocabulary -- what a thing MEANS is dab/model.yaml's
# job, and saying it twice is how two numbers start disagreeing.
endpoints:
  source:
    provider: odata
    service: https://demodata.grapecity.com/northwind/odata/v1
    entity: Orders
    page_size: 100  # the service rejects $top above 100 with a 400
  target:
    platform: duckdb
    models: [historized, current]

ownership:
  team: adss
  upstream: >-
    A public demo OData service. No owner, no SLA and no change notification, so a failing
    contract check is the notification. The recording under das/fixtures is what every build
    reads; the scheduled live run is what says the recording has gone stale.

schema:
  primary_keys: [order_id]
  columns:
    - source_path: OrderId
      target_name: order_id
      type: INTEGER
      mode: REQUIRED
      description: >-
        Edm.Int32. The only property the service metadata marks Nullable=false.
    - source_path: CustomerId
      target_name: customer_id
      type: STRING
      mode: NULLABLE
      description: >-
        Edm.String. Referential constraint to Customers.CustomerId.
    - source_path: EmployeeId
      target_name: employee_id
      type: INTEGER
      mode: NULLABLE
      description: >-
        Edm.Int32. Referential constraint to Employees.EmployeeId.
    - source_path: OrderDate
      target_name: order_date
      type: DATE
      mode: NULLABLE
      description: >-
        Edm.Date. An ISO calendar date with no time part.
    - source_path: RequiredDate
      target_name: required_date
      type: DATE
      mode: NULLABLE
      description: >-
        Edm.Date. An ISO calendar date with no time part.
    - source_path: ShippedDate
      target_name: shipped_date

      mode: NULLABLE
      description: >-
        Edm.Date. Null on records the service has not marked shipped.

      description: >-

173	def _refuse_measures_that_would_share_a_name(uss: Uss) -> None:
174	    """Two events on one entity may not declare the same measure id. ADR 0008.
175	
176	    A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity. While an entity has one event those
177	    are the same thing; with two they are not, and the same id on both emits one column twice
178	    AND silently replaces one definition with the other in the glossary.
179	
180	    The column half would fail the build loudly -- DuckDB renames the second column rather than
181	    raising, so the built table stops matching the published contract. The glossary half is
182	    caught by nothing: no check inspects the definitions, and they are what a question's
183	    references resolve against and what the page renders. A reader would be shown a plausible
184	    sentence about the wrong number, and everything would pass.
185	    """
186	    seen: dict[tuple[str, str], str] = {}
187	    for event in uss.events:
188	        for measure in event.measures:
189	            key = (event.entity_id, measure.id)
190	            if key in seen:
191	                raise UssError(
192	                    f"{event.entity_id} declares {measure.id} on both {seen[key]} and "
193	                    f"{event.id}. A measure is named for its entity and owned by its event, so "
194	                    f"the two would share one column -- and {event.id}'s definition would "
195	                    f"replace {seen[key]}'s in the glossary, which nothing checks and the page "
196	                    f"renders. Give them separate ids, or one definition covering both."
197	                )
198	            seen[key] = event.id

201	def _refuse_measures_of_things_that_are_not_numbers(uss: Uss, model: Model) -> None:
202	    for event in uss.events:
203	        if event.kind is not EventKind.TRANSACTION:
204	            raise UssError(
205	                f"{event.id} is declared {event.kind}, and the generator only builds "
206	                f"transaction stages. It would emit a transaction stage anyway and mark "
207	                f"every row current, which is worse than refusing: nothing downstream could "
208	                f"tell. A snapshot stage arrives in the slice that first needs one."
209	            )
210	        entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
211	        if not entity.attribute(event.date_attribute_id).is_date:
212	            raise UssError(
213	                f"{event.id} is dated by {event.date_attribute_id}, which is not a date."
214	            )
215	        for measure in event.measures:
216	            if measure.attribute_id and not entity.attribute(measure.attribute_id).is_number:
217	                raise UssError(

219	                    f"number. Summing what is not a number produces a number nobody can read."
220	                )

223	def _version_cte(model: Model, event: Event) -> str:
224	    """The version of each entity this event is measured on: the latest in which it is dated."""
225	    entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
226	    date = crossing(event.date_attribute_id)
227	    held = "revision"
228	    lines = [
229	        f"    {held}.{crossing(entity.source_key)} AS {entity.key_column}",
230	        f"    {held}.eff_tmstp AS _observed_at",
231	        f"    cast({held}.{date} AS DATE) AS _event_date",
232	    ]
233	    for measure in event.measures:
234	        column = f"_measure__{entity.object_name}__{measure.id.lower()}"
235	        if measure.aggregate is Aggregate.COUNT:
236	            value = f"cast(1 AS {COUNT_TYPE})"
237	        else:
238	            attribute = crossing(str(measure.attribute_id))
239	            value = f"cast({held}.{attribute} AS {SUM_TYPE})"
240	        lines.append(f"    {value} AS {column}")
241	    selected = ",\n".join(lines)
242	    return (
243	        f"{event.name}__version AS (\n"
244	        f"SELECT\n{selected}\n"
245	        f'FROM dab."view_{entity.id}_hist" AS {held}\n'
246	        f"WHERE {held}.{date} IS NOT NULL\n"
247	        f"QUALIFY row_number() OVER (\n"
248	        f"    PARTITION BY {held}.{crossing(entity.source_key)}\n"
249	        f"    ORDER BY {held}.eff_tmstp DESC\n"
250	        f") = 1\n"
251	        f")"
252	    )

254	
255	def _inherit_cte(model: Model, event: Event, edge: Relationship) -> str:
256	    """One inherited key: the pair in force when the inheriting row was observed. ADR 0006.
257	
258	    Resolved per inheriting ROW rather than per key -- the partition carries the observation
259	    time -- because that is the whole reason ADR 0006 chose the observation time over "now".
260	    A stage that kept more than the latest version of an entity would otherwise hand every one
261	    of those versions the same parent, which is "as of now" wearing the other rule's clothes.
262	
263	    Read from `v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, which is the raw pairs plus the relationship's name, and
264	    ranked here rather than by the engine. The engine's own ranked view answers a different
265	    question -- who the parent is *now* -- and answers it with `rank()`, which returns two rows
266	    for a child whose source named two parents at one instant. Two rows here would double that
267	    child's measures, so the ranking is `row_number()` and the tie is refused by a data check.
268	    """
269	    source = model.entity(edge.source_entity_id)
270	    target = model.entity(edge.target_entity_id)
271	    held = edge.id.lower()
272	    return (
273	        f"{event.name}__{held} AS (\n"
274	        f"SELECT\n"
275	        f"    revision.{source.key_column} AS {source.key_column},\n"
276	        f"    revision._observed_at AS _observed_at,\n"
277	        f"    pair.{crossing(target.source_key)} AS {target.key_column}\n"
278	        f"FROM {event.name}__version AS revision\n"
279	        f'LEFT JOIN dab."v_{edge.id}" AS pair\n'
280	        f"    ON pair.{crossing(source.source_key)} = revision.{source.key_column}\n"
281	        f"    AND pair.rel_name = '{edge.id}'\n"
282	        f"    AND pair.row_st = 'Y'\n"
283	        f"    AND pair.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at\n"
284	        f"QUALIFY row_number() OVER (\n"
285	        f"    PARTITION BY revision.{source.key_column}, revision._observed_at\n"
286	        f"    ORDER BY\n"
287	        f"        pair.eff_tmstp DESC,\n"
288	        f"        pair.ver_tmstp DESC,\n"
289	        f"        pair.{crossing(target.source_key)}\n"
290	        f") = 1\n"
291	        f")"
292	    )

294	
295	def _stage_cte(model: Model, event: Event) -> str:
296	    """One stage: the entity's version, with the key of everything it inherits from."""
297	    entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
298	    edges = model.edges_from(entity.id)
299	    lines = [
300	        f"    revision.{entity.key_column} AS {entity.key_column}",
301	        "    revision._observed_at AS _observed_at",
302	        "    revision._event_date AS _event_date",
303	    ]
304	    lines += [
305	        f"    {edge.id.lower()}.{model.entity(edge.target_entity_id).key_column} "
306	        f"AS {model.entity(edge.target_entity_id).key_column}"
307	        for edge in edges
308	    ]
309	    lines += [
310	        f"    revision._measure__{entity.object_name}__{measure.id.lower()} "
311	        f"AS _measure__{entity.object_name}__{measure.id.lower()}"
312	        for measure in event.measures
313	    ]
314	    # One row per inheriting row in each of these, so none of the joins can fan out. LEFT
315	    # anyway: the row that inherits nothing is kept by the join inside the CTE, and an inner
316	    # join here would undo that one level up.
317	    joins = "".join(
318	        f"\nLEFT JOIN {event.name}__{edge.id.lower()} AS {edge.id.lower()}\n"
319	        f"    ON {edge.id.lower()}.{entity.key_column} = revision.{entity.key_column}\n"
320	        f"    AND {edge.id.lower()}._observed_at = revision._observed_at"
321	        for edge in edges
322	    )
323	    selected = ",\n".join(lines)
324	    return (
325	        f"{event.name} AS (\nSELECT\n{selected}\nFROM {event.name}__version AS revision{joins}\n)"
326	    )

328	
329	def _branch(model: Model, uss: Uss, event: Event, keys: tuple[str, ...]) -> str:
330	    """One branch of the union: this stage's own columns, and a typed NULL for the rest."""
331	    entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
332	    carried = {entity.key_column} | {
333	        model.entity(edge.target_entity_id).key_column for edge in model.edges_from(entity.id)
334	    }
335	    lines = [
336	        f"    '{entity.object_name}' AS _stage",
337	        f"    '{event.name}' AS _event",
338	        f"    {event.name}._event_date AS _event_date",
339	        "    TRUE AS _is_current",
340	        f"    {event.name}._observed_at AS _observed_at",
341	    ]
342	    for key in keys:
343	        value = f"{event.name}.{key}" if key in carried else "cast(NULL AS VARCHAR)"
344	        lines.append(f"    {value} AS {key}")
345	    owned = {column for candidate, _, column in uss.measure_columns() if candidate is event}
346	    for _, measure, column in uss.measure_columns():
347	        value = f"{event.name}.{column}" if column in owned else f"cast(NULL AS {measure.sql_type})"
348	        lines.append(f"    {value} AS {column}")
349	    return "SELECT\n" + ",\n".join(lines) + f"\nFROM {event.name} AS {event.name}"

351	
352	def entity_ids(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> tuple[str, ...]:
353	    """Every entity the bridge names, in MODEL order: the ones with events, and the ones they
354	    inherit from. An entity reached only by inheritance still needs a peripheral, or the bridge
355	    carries a key that joins to nothing.
356	    """
357	    touched = {event.entity_id for event in uss.events}
358	    touched |= {
359	        edge.target_entity_id for event in uss.events for edge in model.edges_from(event.entity_id)
360	    }
361	    return tuple(entity.id for entity in model.entities if entity.id in touched)
362	
363	
364	def entity_keys(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> tuple[str, ...]:
365	    """One key column per entity the bridge names, in MODEL order.
366	
367	    Model order, not event order: reordering two events in the sidecar is not a model change,
368	    and it must not rearrange a contract that consumers are written against. The check cannot
369	    catch that on its own, because it derives what it expects from this same function.
370	    """
371	    return tuple(model.entity(entity_id).key_column for entity_id in entity_ids(model, uss))
372	
373	
374	def bridge_columns(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> tuple[str, ...]:
375	    """The published column contract, in order.
376	
377	    Grouped: the structural columns, then one key per entity in model order, then one column
378	    per measure in declaration order.
379	
380	    That grouping means the contract does NOT only ever grow at the end, and saying otherwise
381	    would be the more comfortable lie. A new entity appends a key, and because keys precede
382	    measures, every measure column moves right. An entity inserted in the middle of the model
383	    moves the keys after it as well. So the model file's own order is part of this contract,
384	    and nothing here can catch a rearrangement: the check that compares the built bridge to
385	    this contract derives what it expects from this same function, so both sides move together
386	    and it passes either way.
387	
388	    What makes that tolerable rather than a defect is that nothing reads this table by
389	    position. Conventions section 3 forbids `SELECT *`, the questions name their columns and
390	    so does the destination. A consumer that did read positionally would be reading a contract
391	    this docstring does not offer it. New entities still go at the end, because moving a key
392	    column is a bigger change than moving a measure. Blueprint B7.
393	    """
394	    keys = entity_keys(model, uss)
395	    structural = ("_stage", "_event", "_event_date", "_is_current", "_observed_at")
396	    return structural + keys + tuple(column for _, _, column in uss.measure_columns())

399	def bridge_sql(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> str:
400	    """One row per measurement event, over every stage the declarations name."""
401	    keys = entity_keys(model, uss)
402	    ctes = ",\n\n".join(
403	        cte
404	        for event in uss.events
405	        for cte in (
406	            _version_cte(model, event),
407	            *(_inherit_cte(model, event, edge) for edge in model.edges_from(event.entity_id)),
408	            _stage_cte(model, event),
409	        )
410	    )
411	    branches = "\n\nUNION ALL\n\n".join(_branch(model, uss, event, keys) for event in uss.events)
412	    return f"{_GENERATED}\nCREATE OR REPLACE TABLE {BRIDGE.sql} AS\nWITH {ctes}\n\n{branches};\n"
413	
414	
415	def peripheral_sql(model: Model, entity_id: str) -> str:
416	    """One row per entity instance, current state, key first and attributes as declared."""
417	    entity: Entity = model.entity(entity_id)
418	    lines = [
419	        f"    e.{crossing(entity.source_key)} AS {entity.key_column}",
420	        "    e.eff_tmstp AS _observed_at",
421	    ]
422	    lines += [f"    e.{crossing(a.id)} AS {a.column}" for a in entity.attributes]
423	    selected = ",\n".join(lines)
424	    relation = Relation(Schema.DAR_USS, entity.object_name)
425	    return (
426	        f"{_GENERATED}\n"
427	        f"CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE {relation.sql} AS\n"
428	        f"SELECT\n{selected}\n"
429	        f'FROM dab."view_{entity.id}_hist" AS e\n'
430	        f"QUALIFY row_number() OVER (\n"
431	        f"    PARTITION BY e.{crossing(entity.source_key)}\n"
432	        f"    ORDER BY e.eff_tmstp DESC\n"
433	        f") = 1;\n"
434	    )

437	def calendar_sql() -> str:
438	    """Dense and daily across everything the bridge holds. Civil arithmetic only.
439	
440	    A calendar containing only the days something happened is not a calendar: a month with
441	    no events must still appear in a time series. Fiscal periods and holidays are business
442	    meaning and would need a definition, so they belong in the model, not in a generator.
443	    """
444	    return (
445	        f"{_GENERATED}\n"
446	        f"CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE {CALENDAR.sql} AS\n"
447	        f"WITH bounds AS (\n"
448	        f"SELECT\n"
449	        f"    min(b._event_date) AS first_date,\n"
450	        f"    max(b._event_date) AS last_date\n"
451	        f"FROM {BRIDGE.sql} AS b\n"
452	        f"),\n\n"
453	        f"every_day AS (\n"
454	        f"SELECT\n"
455	        f"    cast(d.day AS DATE) AS date_key\n"
456	        f"FROM bounds AS bo\n"
457	        f"CROSS JOIN range(\n"
458	        f"    bo.first_date, bo.last_date + INTERVAL 1 DAY, INTERVAL 1 DAY\n"
459	        f") AS d (day)\n"
460	        f")\n\n"
461	        f"SELECT\n"
462	        f"    d.date_key AS date_key,\n"
463	        f"    cast(year(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS year_number,\n"
464	        f"    cast(quarter(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS quarter_of_year,\n"
465	        f"    cast(month(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS month_of_year,\n"
466	        f"    cast(day(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS day_of_month,\n"
467	        f"    cast(date_trunc('year', d.date_key) AS DATE) AS year_start,\n"
468	        f"    cast(date_trunc('quarter', d.date_key) AS DATE) AS quarter_start,\n"
469	        f"    cast(date_trunc('month', d.date_key) AS DATE) AS month_start,\n"
470	        f"    strftime(d.date_key, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(d.date_key) AS VARCHAR) "
471	        f"AS quarter_label,\n"
472	        f"    strftime(d.date_key, '%Y-%m') AS month_label\n"
473	        f"FROM every_day AS d;\n"
474	    )

477	def definitions(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> dict[str, str]:
478	    """Every definition, by the token that refers to it. Copied verbatim, never composed.
479	
480	    A generator that composed a definition would be a third place the data is explained,
481	    and the worst kind: one nobody wrote and nobody reviews.
482	    """
483	    found = dict(model.definitions())
484	    for event in uss.events:
485	        found[f"{event.entity_id}.events.{event.id}"] = event.definition
486	        for measure in event.measures:
487	            found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
488	    return found
